title: Blood sugar spikes are not necessarily bad for you
content:
It's trendy to be concerned about blood sugar spikes, but these can be a normal response to eating. Here's when you don't need to worry.
Over the last few years, two surprising things have started happening.
Normal, otherwise healthy people have started wearing devices that allow them to check their blood sugar levels throughout the day. Others have been cutting out refined carbohydrates such as white bread and pasta entirely.
In fact, authors, podcasters and wellness influencers have been selling the idea that we all need to check for blood sugar spikes and avoid them. According to this extreme view, we allow significant amounts of glucose in the bloodstream at our peril. Even in healthy people with no metabolic diseases, to risk a blood sugar spike is, they say, to welcome hormonal imbalances, acne, mood swings, and worse.
But now experts are pushing back. Here's when to worry, and when that carbohydrate-heavy meal is unlikely to do any lasting damage.
When we eat and digest sugary foods, such as refined sugar, fruit and carbohydrate-rich food, our blood sugar naturally inclines.
That's because as we digest carbohydrates and sugars, they are broken down into glucose, which is then absorbed into the bloodstream, temporarily leading our blood sugar levels to rise. As it does so, the pancreas responds by secreting the hormone insulin , which helps move the glucose out of our bloodstream and into the body's cells to provide energy.
It's not only food that can raise our blood glucose levels. During high-intensity exercise, hormones such as adrenaline signal the liver to release more glucose into the bloodstream, providing extra fuel for working muscles. As a result, blood glucose can temporarily rise, says Jennifer Sherr, a paediatric endocrinologist from Yale School of Medicine, Connecticut in the US.
In people with diabetes the body does not produce enough insulin, or it no longer works as it should (insulin resistance). This means that after eating, their blood sugar can become dangerously high. In this case, it's essential that people carefully manage their diet, exercise, and monitor their blood sugar levels to avoid spikes. Some people also need to take medications such as insulin or metformin.
Among healthy individuals, a rise in blood glucose after eating is a normal physiological response . "The biggest misconception is that every glucose spike is harmful," says Adrian Brown, associate professor in nutrition and dietetics from University College London in the UK.
Recently I experimented with giving up added sugar for six weeks ( read more from the BBC on what I learned ) . Since then, I've been especially attuned to the fact that when I eat sugary foods, my blood sugar is bound to rise .
Our blood sugar level typically peaks around one hour after eating and tends to return to baseline within the next two hours . If a spike is brief and occurs in someone with a normal metabolism, we should not be concerned, says Brown.
It's when blood glucose remains elevated for longer than expected that it could indicate that the body is not regulating glucose normally, says Sherr. This could be a sign of insulin resistance, where the body doesn't respond to glucose normally. Insulin resistance can happen if the body is exposed to high blood sugar levels over a long period of time. Eventually it can lead to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes. The persistently high blood glucose experienced by some diabetics can then lead to complications including nerve and eye damage, heart disease and stroke.
However some experts argue that there is not enough evidence to say that excessive blood glucose leads to insulin resistance directly. Instead, the explanation could be that when we eat more than our body needs these excess calories tend to be converted to fat , says Nicola Guess, a dietician and senior research fellow at the University of Oxford in the UK. The resulting weight gain is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, she adds.
People with diabetes already monitor their blood sugar regularly. One way they do this is with continuous blood sugar monitors (CGMs), which measure blood sugar levels throughout the day.
There's now a growing commercial market for these devices in otherwise healthy people. However, some experts warn that they are unnecessary for those without diabetes . One study of non-diabetic participants found that their blood sugar levels were in the healthy range 96% of the time, for instance.

title: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia
content:
President Donald Trump says the US is looking "very strongly" at the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was watching closely amid concerns the incident could lead to the spread of pneumonic plague, but there was no cause for alarm.
Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".
Unconfirmed reports suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
Asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague spreading from Russia, Trump said he had not spoken to the Kremlin about it.
"I hate to see them having it," he said, but added: "We'll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help."
No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since the lab technician's death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.
The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.
Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.
Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature.
"If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."
The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.
The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis , which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death , is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East was founded just over 100 years ago.
Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.
"Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.
He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here."
"People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said.
"It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."

title: Nobel Prize awarded for revealing inner workings of the brain
content:
US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in the field of optogenetics.
Their research has helped scientists learn more about the inner workings of the brain, to better understand how the human mind works.
The Nobel Committee praised the trio for laying the foundation of a new era in neuroscience by revealing how to switch on and off neural circuits behind "specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders".
In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method to try to restore sight in people with visual impairment .
"Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain," the Nobel Assembly said.
"Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity's great mysteries: how our incredible brain works."
The winners said it was "absolutely wonderful" to get the award, and that it was an honour to share the accolade with friends.
The three men will also share the £900,000 (12 million Swedish kronor) prize money.
Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, explained: "Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of."
Before, the inner workings behind feelings, behaviours and bodily functions were more of a mystery to scientists.
Optogenetics is a way to illuminate brain pathways, using a special protein borrowed from algae that scientists use to control cell electrical activity using light.
In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, the algal protein with unique properties.
Deisseroth worked out how to use this light controlled protein to switch on nerve cells in the brains of mice.
Researchers have since been able to study nerve cells and pathways in animals to see and discover more about what they do.
The Nobel Committee said: "Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in the brain. They can bring memories to life, create feelings, drive behaviours and study the types of neurons that are involved in various psychiatric and neurological disorders."
That is providing important insights into how the nervous system interacts with various cells in other areas of the body, such as in the heart and gut, the committee added.
Researchers have also taken "the first steps" towards using optogenetics as a medical treatment, the committee explained.
In ongoing clinical trials, scientists have been working to restore vision in people who have become blind due to retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys the eye's rods and cones.
By inserting a special protein in the damaged region of the eye, the patient regained some vision when wearing special glasses emitting light. This switched on the therapeutic algae proteins.
Belgian physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space.

title: WHO reinforces oral disease surveillance with an updated NCD STEPS module
content:
A new publication in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization presents the revised WHO oral health module for the STEPwise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance (STEPS). The updated module introduces a more contemporary and practical approach to collecting population-level data on oral diseases, helping countries generate the evidence needed to inform policy and strengthen monitoring of oral health program and policy implementation.
The WHO STEPwise framework is a well-established and widely used standardized approach for collecting data on behavioural and biological risk factors of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), including oral diseases. Recognizing the gap in reliable and policy-relevant oral health data, WHO revised the oral health module in 2024 to better support national surveillance systems and align with current global monitoring priorities.
"The updated STEPS Oral Health Module gives countries a practical way to integrate oral diseases into broader NCD surveillance. By generating data on oral diseases alongside other NCDs and their shared risk factors, it provides the evidence needed for better decision-making, more effective prevention strategies and stronger health systems,” said Dr Søren Brostrøm, Director, Department of Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental Health, WHO.
A key innovation of the revised module is its feasibility for implementation within routine STEPS surveys. The streamlined questionnaire and simplified clinical assessment have been designed so that data collection can be carried out by trained survey staff who are not oral health specialists. By combining self-reported information with a simple clinical assessment in a representative sample, the module supports evidence-informed decision-making and contributes to stronger monitoring of oral diseases as part of broader noncommunicable disease surveillance systems. The updated module is the result of a collaborative effort involving international experts and WHO collaborating centres and reflects the latest evidence on oral disease measurement, surveillance and public health priorities.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in physics has been awarded to Francis Halzen, a pioneering Belgian astrophysicist whose work developing a massive observatory in Antarctica to detect “ghostly” cosmic particles laid the foundations for an “entirely new type of astronomy.” The physics prize was announced on Tuesday at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm. “Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument,” said Nobel committee chair Mark Pearce in a statement. “His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.” Halzen told the Nobel news conference by phone from Italy that it was a “great surprise” and “pleasure” to win the award. “When we started this project, everybody realized this was maybe a good idea but very few thought it would work, including myself,” he said. “So this was kind of an adventure where success wasn’t guaranteed.” Halzen, a professor based at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, first presented plans for this observatory – now called the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – in 1988, envisioning a vast apparatus in the Antarctic ice that could capture particles known as neutrinos. The observatory harnesses a key property of neutrinos; namely that they produce a flash of light when colliding with an atomic nucleus which could be tracked by sensors embedded in clear, glacial ice. Arriving at Earth from the far reaches of the cosmos, neutrinos are often called “ghostly” because they are extremely volatile, or vaporous, and can go through any kind of matter without changing. They have almost no mass, and no electrical charge. They can travel through the most extreme environments, like stars, planets and entire galaxies, and remain the same. “It’s been a while since the Nobel Prize has gone to a single individual and that points to the uniqueness of his vision,” said Richard Fitzgerald, editor-in-chief of Physics Today, which is published by the American Institute of Physics. “It took a team of hundreds of people to build it, but it all started with one person.” This is a developing story and will be updated.
